items.title: $5 Million Paid, One Federal Lawsuit: Inside the Justice Department's Challenge to Evanston's Reparations Program
items.body:
## A First-of-Its-Kind Program Faces Its Biggest Test

In 2019, the Evanston, Illinois City Council did something no U.S. municipality had done before: it voted to fund a local reparations program for Black residents harmed by decades of housing discrimination and redlining. Seven years later, that program is at the center of a federal legal battle that could shape whether any American city can run a race-based reparations effort at all.

The U.S. Department of Justice has moved to intervene in a lawsuit against the city, arguing that Evanston's program amounts to unconstitutional racial discrimination. The case is being watched closely far beyond Illinois, since Evanston's program has long served as a model — and a test case — for reparations advocates across the country.

## How Evanston's Program Works

Evanston's "Restorative Housing Program" grew out of a 2019 City Council decision to dedicate the first $10 million collected from the city's 3% cannabis sales tax to reparations efforts. Approved in March 2021, the program offers qualifying Black residents grants of up to $25,000 that can be used toward a down payment, mortgage assistance or home repairs.

To qualify, applicants must have lived in Evanston between 1919 and 1969 — the period during which the city enforced discriminatory housing policies — or be a direct descendant of someone who did. The city has said the program is meant to address documented harm from redlining and other housing discrimination, not to serve as a general benefit based on race alone.

According to court filings, the city has distributed more than $5 million to date, with additional payments planned as funding becomes available. Early rounds of the program provided $25,000 each to dozens of residents, and city officials have said funding constraints — including softer-than-expected cannabis tax revenue — have slowed the pace of payments.

## The Lawsuit That Started It All

The legal challenge began in 2024, when a group of Evanston residents and descendants of former residents who are not Black filed suit in federal court. The case, *Flinn v. City of Evanston*, argues that excluding non-Black applicants from the program violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, which generally bars government programs from distributing benefits based on race.

The city sought to have the case dismissed, arguing the program was a narrowly tailored remedy for specific, documented discrimination rather than a broad racial preference. A federal judge rejected that motion in March 2026, allowing the case to proceed — a ruling that opened the door for the Justice Department's involvement.

## Why the DOJ Stepped In

Shortly after the dismissal was denied, the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division opened its own investigation into the Evanston program under the Equal Protection Clause and the federal Fair Housing Act. The department has said the city declined to cooperate with that inquiry, which prompted federal attorneys to seek to formally intervene in the private lawsuit rather than pursue a separate case.

In its filings, the DOJ contends the government has what it calls an "unconditional right" to intervene in cases alleging the denial of equal protection based on race, and argues Evanston's program distributes cash and housing assistance "solely" on the basis of an applicant's race, rather than on individualized proof of harm. The department's proposed complaint asks the court to find the program unlawful under both the Constitution and federal fair-housing law.

Evanston officials and reparations advocates have pushed back, arguing the program is a targeted remedy grounded in a documented history of the city's own discriminatory housing practices between 1919 and 1969 — not an open-ended racial preference. The city's Reparations Committee has said it remains committed to the program while the litigation continues, and some members have framed the case as a test of whether any local government can ever attempt to repair historical harm through direct, race-conscious remedies.

## Why This Case Matters Beyond Evanston

Evanston's program has been widely cited as a national blueprint since its launch, and other cities and states have looked to it while considering their own reparations proposals. Legal observers note that a ruling against Evanston could make it significantly harder for other municipalities to design similar programs, while a ruling in the city's favor could bolster the legal footing for reparations efforts elsewhere.

The case is still in its early stages in federal district court in Illinois, and a ruling on the merits is not expected imminently. Both the underlying *Flinn* lawsuit and the Justice Department's intervention will need to work through further briefing and, potentially, appeals — meaning the ultimate fate of Evanston's program, and its implications for reparations policy nationwide, likely remain months or years away from resolution.

*This article summarizes publicly reported developments in ongoing litigation. It is intended for general informational purposes and does not constitute legal advice or analysis.*

items.title: 5 Dead, One Contract Severed: Inside Amazon's Break With 21 Air After the Deadly Miami Runway Crash
items.body:
Nine days after a Boeing 767 cargo jet overran a runway at Miami International Airport and killed five people on the ground, Amazon has suspended its cargo partnership with 21 Air, the North Carolina-based carrier that operated the flight. The move comes as federal investigators dig into both the mechanics of the crash and the safety record of the airline behind it.

## What happened on the runway

The aircraft, operating as 21 Air Flight 7598 on behalf of Amazon Air, was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, on the afternoon of September 6 when it touched down on Runway 30 and failed to stop before running out of pavement. The jet struck a parked cleaning van operated by a contractor that services aircraft between flights. Seven people were reportedly in or near the vehicle; five were killed and others injured. The crash also sparked a fire that sent a heavy plume of smoke over the airport, prompting a temporary halt to operations at MIA.

## What investigators have found so far

The National Transportation Safety Board has cautioned that it is too early to assign a cause, but data pulled from the plane's flight recorders paints a detailed picture of the final seconds before impact. According to the NTSB's preliminary findings, the aircraft touched down at a groundspeed of roughly 158 knots — well above a typical landing speed for a 767 — and the recorders show no indication that the plane's speed brakes or thrust reversers were ever deployed. Flight data also shows the crew briefly applied the brakes, then released them and pushed the throttles up to power levels consistent with an attempted go-around, before pulling back to idle and reapplying the brakes seconds later. Investigators have said the crew expressed concern about excessive speed during the approach, and that a shift in wind direction around the time of landing may have complicated the crew's ability to slow the aircraft. NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy said a fuller preliminary report is expected in the coming weeks, with a final determination of probable cause likely taking much longer.

## Amazon steps back from 21 Air

In the aftermath, Amazon confirmed it has paused flight operations with 21 Air, one of several regional cargo carriers that fly Boeing 767 freighters branded with the Amazon Air logo under contract. The suspension halts new flights while the NTSB investigation continues, though neither company has said whether the relationship will resume once the inquiry concludes. Homendy has indicated that investigators plan to scrutinize not just the flight crew's actions but the broader relationship between Amazon and 21 Air, including how safety responsibilities and oversight were divided under their contract — a question that could shape how large shippers manage the outside carriers they depend on to move goods.

## Questions about the carrier's safety culture

The crash has also renewed scrutiny of 21 Air itself. Several former employees have come forward in recent days describing what they characterize as a pattern of safety concerns at the carrier that predates the Miami crash, including allegations of deferred maintenance issues and pressure felt by pilots and mechanics who raised objections. Among them is a former 21 Air employee who has an active federal whistleblower lawsuit alleging he was fired in 2022 after repeatedly raising safety concerns internally. It's important to note these are allegations that have not been proven in court, and 21 Air has not publicly detailed a response to each claim. The NTSB has acknowledged it is aware of the allegations as part of its broader review of the carrier's operations and oversight history.

## What comes next

For now, the investigation remains in its early stages. The NTSB's process typically includes a preliminary report focused on factual findings, followed by a much longer review before any formal conclusion on probable cause and contributing factors. Families of those killed, aviation regulators, and Amazon's logistics network will all be watching closely — the outcome could influence not only 21 Air's future but how major shippers vet the safety practices of the cargo carriers they rely on nationwide.

items.title: Saudi Pipeline Strike Cuts Key Oil Lifeline, Pushing Crude Toward $110 a Barrel
items.body:
## A Critical Artery Goes Offline

Global oil markets are on edge after reports of a drone strike on Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline, known as Petroline, one of the few remaining routes capable of moving crude from the kingdom's eastern oil fields to export terminals on the Red Sea without passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Industry sources say the damage has forced Saudi authorities to scale back production and reroute shipments while repair crews assess the extent of the disruption.

The pipeline, which under normal conditions can carry roughly five million barrels of oil and refined products per day, has long been viewed by energy planners as a strategic hedge against exactly the kind of chokepoint risk now playing out in the Strait of Hormuz, where ongoing regional conflict has already curtailed tanker traffic for weeks. With that alternate route now compromised, traders say the market is confronting the possibility that a meaningful share of Gulf export capacity could be constrained at the same time.

## Why Prices Are Reacting

Benchmark crude prices have climbed sharply on the news, with several analysts telling news outlets that a sustained outage could push prices toward the $110-a-barrel mark, a level not tested in years. Energy strategists caution that figures remain fluid and will depend heavily on how quickly Saudi Arabia can restore flows, whether alternative export arrangements can absorb the shortfall, and how other OPEC+ producers respond.

"Markets don't just price in the barrels that are actually lost, they price in the uncertainty of what comes next," one commodities analyst said, reflecting a view echoed across trading desks this week. Shipping and insurance costs for tankers in the wider region have also risen, according to maritime industry sources, adding further upward pressure on landed oil prices for importers.

## Diplomacy Stalls as Stakes Rise

The incident has complicated efforts by regional and international mediators who had been working to de-escalate tensions around the Strait of Hormuz. Several Gulf-focused diplomatic channels have reportedly gone quiet in the immediate aftermath, as governments assess responsibility for the strike and weigh their next moves. Analysts note that any prolonged stalemate raises the risk that both the strait and key overland pipeline routes remain under a cloud of uncertainty simultaneously, a scenario energy security planners have long flagged as a worst-case outcome for global supply.

Saudi officials have not publicly detailed the full scope of repairs, though statements from the kingdom's energy sector emphasize that safeguarding export infrastructure remains a top priority and that contingency measures are being activated.

## What It Means Going Forward

For consumers, a sustained move toward $110 crude would likely translate into higher prices at the pump and added cost pressure across shipping, manufacturing, and travel, sectors already sensitive to energy costs. Central banks and finance ministries in major importing economies are reportedly monitoring the situation closely given the potential knock-on effects for inflation.

Energy analysts caution against overreacting to early, still-developing reports, noting that oil markets have weathered supply shocks before through emergency reserve releases, output adjustments from other producers, and diplomatic de-escalation. Even so, the combination of a disabled bypass route and a still-restricted strait marks one of the more serious tests of Gulf energy security in recent memory, and markets are likely to stay volatile until clearer information emerges on both the pipeline's repair timeline and the broader diplomatic path forward.
